analysis.one_liner: Cuts copyright protection to 28 years, with the cut applied immediately to the largest media companies.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut copyright terms was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and died there without a hearing, vote, or cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed copyright law so that new creative works are protected for 28 years, renewable once for another 28 — instead of the current rule that lasts the author's life plus 70 years. Unusually, it would also apply that shorter term immediately to copyrights owned by giant media and entertainment companies worth more than $150 billion, aimed squarely at the biggest players (only one company, Disney, fits the description). The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the public would have gained: books, music, films, and characters would become free for anyone to use, adapt, and republish decades earlier than under current law. Libraries, teachers, small creators, and fans who today must license or wait out terms lasting close to a century would get access sooner. Companies holding very old media catalogs — above all Disney's aging film and character library — would have lost those exclusive rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Libraries, creators, and the public domain

how_it_helps.text: It shortens new copyrights to 28 years, renewable once for another 28, so books, music, and films would enter the public domain and become free for anyone to copy, adapt, or republish decades sooner.

It applies retroactively to copyrights held by entertainment companies with market capitalization over $150 billion, cutting off those companies' long-tail royalties and returning works to the public sooner.
It protects existing licensees of affected works by letting them keep their licensed rights for a limited transition period (up to 10 years) even after the underlying copyright expires.

analysis.who_pays: Copyright holders would have borne the cost. Big media companies would have seen copyrights on their existing catalogs cut short, and individual creators would have lost the life-plus-70-year term for future works, reducing long-term royalties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Copyright owners, especially big media firms

drawbacks.text: The retroactive cut applies only to companies above a $150 billion market cap in entertainment industries, so an author's book and a rival studio's film would expire on different schedules — the Supreme Court has generally held that Congress may extend or shorten copyright terms, but applying the rule by company size invites challenges that it is an arbitrary, targeted taking of one industry's property.

Shortening terms to 28 years, even prospectively, would sharply reduce the long-term value of creative rights, which critics argue could reduce the incentive to invest in expensive works like films; supporters answer that the Constitution's original copyright terms were 14 years plus a 14-year renewal.

The bill had no cosponsors and no committee action, so its drafting was never examined, and the special treatment of the largest companies makes it look more like a bill aimed at one company than a general copyright reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its merits, the bill would give the public earlier access to creative works, though its retroactive application only to the largest entertainment companies would create two different copyright rules and could face serious constitutional questions about taking existing property rights. But the merits were never tested: no committee held a hearing, no cosponsors joined, and no vote was ever taken, so the public received neither the benefit nor a real debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Steube introduced the bill on June 28, 2022, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no hearing, no vote in committee, and no vote on the House floor.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, meaning the existing copyright terms, including the long terms held by the largest media companies, remained unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large media and entertainment companies kept their existing long copyright terms, including rights to aging catalogs and characters, since the bill died without a hearing or vote. Ordinary people gained nothing and continue to wait decades for works to enter the public domain.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large media companies that kept long copyrights

for.name: Rep. W. Gregory Steube
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to shorten copyright terms, including retroactively for the largest media companies.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after its referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Large motion picture and entertainment conglomerates (over $150 billion market cap)
industries.note: Their existing copyrights would be cut to 28 years, ending long-term ownership of aging catalogs like classic films and characters. This provision is aimed at the largest players, notably the one U.S. media company of that size.

Their future works would also get only 28 years (plus one renewal) instead of life plus 70, substantially reducing long-term royalties for individual creators too. Unlike the biggest companies, they would also lose their current long terms only for new works.

industries.industry: Public domain users: libraries, archives, remix artists, streaming and adaptation startups
industries.note: Works would become free to reuse decades sooner, cutting licensing costs for schools, creators, and small media companies.
